key_insight: Correlations in the data—not just sparsity or idealized independence—determine how models hide features in superposition; data statistics shape a predictable geometry of overlapping feature vectors rather than random interference.
problem_solved: Explains how and why neural networks arrange more features than dimensions (superposition) on realistic, correlated datasets, resolving the gap between idealized theory and practical representations.
method: Analytical framework that links data second-order statistics (covariance/correlations) to the geometric arrangement of learned feature vectors.
Controlled experiments on synthetic and real datasets to measure how changing correlation structure alters feature overlap, alignment, and interference.
Quantitative visualizations and metrics that map data correlation matrices to observable feature-geometry patterns in trained models.
impact: Provides practitioners and interpretability researchers with a principled way to predict and diagnose feature superposition from dataset statistics, improving model analysis, compression, and feature decoding strategies.
visual_elements: Schematic comparing orthogonal vs. superposed feature vectors in high-dimensional space, annotated to show correlation-driven clustering/alignment.
Paired heatmaps: data correlation matrix vs. learned feature overlap matrix to show one-to-one structural relationships.
Line/bar charts showing how varying correlation strength changes interference, feature sparsity, and task performance.
Flow diagram: data statistics → theoretical prediction of geometry → empirical measurement on models.
paper_title: From Data Statistics to Feature Geometry: How Correlations Shape Superposition
paper_authors: Lucas Prieto, Edward Stevinson, Melih Barsbey, Tolga Birdal, Pedro A. M. Mediano
